title: Parcelbird — quick-commerce entry
decision_question: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?

initial_hypothesis.statement: Enter now: the market grows 40%+ a year and density will make unit economics positive by month 18.
initial_hypothesis.explanation: Contribution per order is negative at benchmark median ($-6.17), at the best observed density ($-3.44) and even combining best density with the best AOV ($-1.76), before customer acquisition and overhead. Break-even AOV at the best density is about $50.37. The founders' +$2.02 relies on every input beating the best observed site. Growth does not fix structurally negative unit economics, and the plan would consume most of the cash. A good answer rejects the hypothesis (or limits it to a capped, capital-light test with kill criteria). The Zipcart fee evidence shows the economics are not impossible at very high density with a fee, which makes a capped, capital-light test (R2) more defensible — but not the three-city plan.

key_insights.text: Per-order contribution: median $-6.17 (rider $7.40, store $3.50); best observed density $-3.44; best density + best AOV $-1.76. Negative in every observed case.
The founders' plan (+$2.02) needs AOV $45, 3.5 orders/rider-hour, 1,800 orders/day and 2% promotions — each beyond the best observed site; break-even AOV at best observed density is ≈ $50.37.
The pop-up's contribution was about $-12.57 per order (AOV $31, 12% promotions, 2.1 orders/rider-hour, 280 orders/day) — the 18% weekly order growth is promotion-fuelled top-line growth.
Market growth (CAGR 41.5% 2022–25) coexists with structural losses: both incumbents have negative contribution per order and QuickBasket closed 4 of 11 cities.

Capital: $9.5M of the $12.0M cash to month 18 would leave ≈ $2.5M, far below 12 months of runway (≈ $4.8M at the current $0.4M/month burn) — breaking the runway constraint even if the plan works; no follow-on funding expected.
Customer economics are weak: CAC $38 and 22% month-3 retention; at negative contribution per order no customer ever pays back.
The better path: grow the 81%-gross-margin software business — 37 grocers in pipeline (9 late stage, ~$96K ACV), several wanting their own fast delivery, i.e. sell the picks and shovels.
Stated intent (44% weekly) is not demand at a price; and rider pay rules are a further downside risk.

Engages with the evidence that partly supports the founders: with a $3.99 fee and 1% promotions, a site at the best observed density would make about $2.25 per order, but a benchmark-median site still loses about $-0.48 (about $-1.05 if volume falls 14% as at Zipcart), before acquisition cost; Parcelbird's own pop-up ran far below median density. Positive unit economics are possible only at density no Parcelbird site has shown, and the runway constraint is broken regardless.

required_calculations.text: Contribution per order at benchmark median
Contribution at best observed density (and/or best AOV)

required_calculations.expected: $12.0M − $9.5M = $2.5M, about 6 months at $0.4M/month vs 12 months required

decision_relevant_evidence.text: Per-order benchmark inputs and the best observed site
Incumbent losses and QuickBasket city exits
Cash, burn and runway constraint; no follow-on funding
Pop-up test: low AOV, high promotions, low density

contradictory_evidence: Fast market growth and 18% weekly pop-up growth vs negative unit economics
Survey intent (44% weekly) vs retention (22% at month three)
Founders' model vs benchmark and best observed inputs
Zipcart's positive contribution in its densest city (after a fee and promo cut) vs negative economics elsewhere

reasoning_traps.text: 'The market is growing fast, so enter'
'Scale/density will fix the economics' without checking the best observed case
Taking the founders' assumptions or the survey at face value
Treating promotion-fuelled order growth as validation
Ignoring the runway constraint and opportunity cost to the software business
Either ignoring the Zipcart fee evidence, or treating it as proof the plan works without checking density, the volume loss and the runway

key_tradeoffs.text: Growth market upside vs structurally negative unit economics
Becoming an operator vs staying a software supplier (focus, capital)
Learning from a test vs consuming runway

plausible_recommendations.text: Do not launch; focus capital on the software business and sell to grocers launching fast delivery.

A small, capped, capital-light test (e.g. with a grocer partner's existing store, no own dark stores) with explicit kill criteria tied to contribution per order — defensible only if it shows why it cannot become the founders' plan by stealth.
Launch in three cities as planned.
Launch in one city 'to prove density' without showing that even the best observed density loses money.

defensibility_criteria: Computes per-order contribution under realistic (benchmark/best observed) inputs
Offers the software alternative or an explicitly capped test
